title: OpenAI adds 55 school districts to ChatGPT for Teachers, crossing 340,000 educators
subtitle: The new cohort — Baltimore City, Boise, Kamehameha, Northside San Antonio, Sarasota County, and Virginia Beach among them — brings the program to 30 states and roughly two million students.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI has expanded its free ChatGPT for Teachers program with 55 additional school systems across 20 states, adding more than 100,000 educators and support staff. The new cohort includes Baltimore City Public Schools, Boise School District, Kamehameha Schools in Hawai'i, Northside Independent School District in San Antonio, Sarasota County Schools in Florida, and Virginia Beach City Public Schools, alongside Houston ISD, which announced its own expanded rollout on August 27. With this round, OpenAI says it now works with more than 100 K–12 organizations in 30 states, covering about 340,000 educators and staff who serve more than two million students.

The mechanism is a district-administered ChatGPT tenant. Teachers get access to a version of ChatGPT with district-level admin controls, saved lesson templates, and OpenAI's education-tier data protections — no training on their prompts, no cross-district data sharing, and a shared library of vetted 'moves' for lesson planning, family communications, and substitute-teacher notes. It is a materially different product from a personal ChatGPT account: the district owns the workspace, sets the guardrails, and can see aggregate usage without reading individual chats.

This is now the third quarter in a row that OpenAI has traded free educator access for a formal K–12 relationship, following similar moves by Anthropic's Claude for Teachers and Google's Gemini for Education. The competitive pressure is one story; the deployment pattern is another. Every one of these programs installs a governed, admin-controlled AI tenant inside a public school system before any state ed-tech procurement rule has clearly settled how those tenants should be reviewed, contracted, or audited. That gap is starting to show up in the state AI-in-schools bills that are moving in California, Illinois, and Idaho.

Takeaway for learners: if you are a teacher, administrator, or district technology lead, the interesting question is not 'is my district on the list' — it is 'who owns the workspace and the retention settings if we are.' The default educator tier bakes in data protections that a personal account does not have, but the value of those protections depends on a district-level agreement your school has signed. Ask to see it. The same question applies at any organization where a free AI tenant lands before the procurement paperwork catches up.
